units.translation: the abysmal sea of ruin is not easy to cross
a great sea of evils has burst forth
The Attic form of the future πελάσω [I will approach] is πελῶ [I will approach], on which see Thes. vol. 6 p. 687,
Transitive: I cause to approach, I bring near.
The middle form πελάζομαι [I approach] means I approach, I come near.
Does not Zeus approach the fair-horned ox?
having cruelly brought near with unbreakable bonds
calling upon you with god-heard prayers, we approach
It is a poetic present form, which is read twice in Euripides (Rhes. 557, El. 1293) and in Aristophanes imitating tragic speech Thesm. 58. Another poetic form is πλάθω [I approach], which see.
Why do you not come to my aid?
a cake offered to the gods
that which is congealed (τὸ πεπηγός [the congealed thing]), a thick liquid.

πέλανος [a cake] in the manuscripts of various writers is proparoxytone, as can be seen in Thes. vol. 6 p. 689. The correct accent, as it seems, πελανός [a cake] is consistently preserved by M, πελανόν [a cake (acc.)] πελανός [a cake (nom.)] πελανῷ [a cake (dat.)] in the places cited above, except that in two, the accent is double: πέλανός [a cake] Pers. 816 and πέλανόν [a cake (acc.)] ib. 524. Herodianus confirms this in Arcadius p. 64, 13, where he deals with nouns ending in -ανος, σεσημείωται τὸ πελανός [the word πελανός is marked as exceptional]. Eustathius p. 1601, 4 mentions both accents: θυσιῶν ἃς πέλάνους τινές φασιν ἢ καὶ ὀξυτόνως πελανούς [sacrifices which some call πέλανοι or, with acute accent, πελανοί].
wishing to sacrifice a cake to the averting deities
I will come bringing a cake from my house
pouring this cake on my father's tomb
to drink the red cake from living limbs
for so great was the blood-dripping cake
being treated with pure ointment with soft guileless consolations, with a royal cake from the inner sanctuary
M, πελανόν [a cake (acc.)] πελανός [a cake (nom.)] πελανῷ [a cake (dat.)]
the word πελανός is marked as exceptional
sacrifices which some call πέλανοι or, with acute accent, πελανοί
With the article ὁ πέλας [the one near] means neighbor, and more frequently in the plural οἱ πέλας [those near] meaning other people.
On both see Thes. vol. 6 p. 691. Aeschylus used only the plural, οἱ πέλας [those near].
What is this rustling of birds I hear near?
and near are three sisters of these
I think she now stands near him
it seems now her neck is about to fall near the razor's edge
near is present as witness the child of Olympian Zeus
if there is someone near of the bird-seers
to open the house of Artemis near
and near are these sisters of brothers
having been placed near the altar of Zeus Ktesios
like a cock near a hen
I would wish now to have seats near you
you are better at instructing those near
